name: The Antinomies of Pure Reason
plain_explanation: Kant claims that if we try to apply space, time, or the categories to the world as a whole (rather than to objects of possible experience), we get pairs of contradictory conclusions that both seem provable -- for example, that the world both does and does not have a beginning in time and a limit in space.
precise_definition: Four pairs of thesis-and-antithesis arguments, each apparently demonstrable, that arise from illegitimately extending space, time, or the categories beyond possible experience to 'things in general': (1) the world has/has not a beginning in time and limits in space; (2) every composite substance is/is not made of simple parts; (3) there is/is not a causality of freedom in addition to natural causality; (4) there is/is not an absolutely necessary Being.
why_it_mattered: Russell notes this part of the Critique 'greatly influenced Hegel, whose dialectic proceeds wholly by way of antinomies.'
historical_origin: Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic.
examples: First antinomy: the world has a beginning in time and is limited in space (thesis) vs. the world has no beginning and is infinite in time and space (antithesis)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly shaped Hegel's dialectical method of thesis-antithesis-synthesis.
